title: Variations in soil erodibility (K-factor) for the Chernozems depending on the method of texture determination
author: Komissarov, Fomicheva, et al.

steps.title: Collect soil samples in field
steps.instruction: Randomly collect 107 topsoil samples (0–25 cm depth) from croplands over ~10 000 ha using a hand Edelman drill (5 cm diameter); for each point record GPS coordinates and take a mixed sample of three repetitions; also drill to the illuvial B horizon to ~1 m depth for diagnostic purposes.

steps.title: Dry, crush and sieve samples
steps.instruction: In the laboratory dry each soil sample in an oven at 90 °C until constant weight, then crush and pass through a sieve to obtain a fine, homogeneous material for analysis.

steps.title: Determine soil organic carbon (SOC)
steps.instruction: Measure SOC by the Tyurin method using a Specord M40 spectrophotometer (VEB Carl Zeiss, Germany).

steps.title: Prepare samples for laser diffraction
steps.instruction: For each dried sample: (i) place the undisturbed soil in distilled water and treat in an ultrasonic bath (Vilitek VBS‑1H, 40 kHz) for 5 min; (ii) separate particles larger than 0.1 mm by wet sieving; (iii) prepare three suspensions of the <0.1 mm fraction at concentrations of 80 %, 50 % and 30 % for analysis.

steps.title: Measure particle size by laser diffraction
steps.instruction: Analyze each suspension on a Laska‑TD laser particle size analyzer (Biomedical Systems, Russia) which measures particles from 1 µm to 1000 µm with a 670 nm laser; record the fractions classified as clay (<0.002 mm), silt (0.002–0.05 mm) and very fine sand (0.05–0.1 mm) according to the Atterberg classification.

steps.title: Prepare samples for sedimentation (pipette) method
steps.instruction: Follow GOST 12536: disperse soil in water, allow settling, and separate the fractions defined by the Kachinsky classification – clay (<0.001 mm), very fine silt (0.001–0.005 mm), medium silt (0.005–0.01 mm), very fine sand (0.01–0.05 mm), fine sand (0.05–0.25 mm), coarse sand (0.25–1.0 mm).

steps.title: Convert sedimentation fractions to Atterberg classes
steps.instruction: Apply Shein’s method: assume a linear cumulative distribution between 0.001 mm and 0.005 mm; recalculate fractions <0.002 mm and 0.002–0.05 mm proportionally; use only fractions <0.1 mm, scaling their total to 100 %.

steps.title: Calculate textural factor M
steps.instruction: For each sample compute M = (msilt + mvfs) × (100 − mc), where mc is clay (%) (<0.002 mm), msilt is silt (%) (0.002–0.05 mm) and mvfs is very fine sand (%) (0.05–0.1 mm) obtained from either laser diffraction or sedimentation data.

steps.title: Compute K‑factor using RUSLE formula
steps.instruction: Insert the values into K = [(2.1 × 10⁻⁴ · M¹·¹⁴ · (12 − OM) + 3.25 · (s − 2) + 25 · (p − 3)/100] × 0.1317, where OM is organic matter (%) from the Tyurin SOC analysis, s is soil‑structure class (1 = very fine granular, 2 = fine granular, 3 = medium/coarse granular, 4 = blocky/platy/massive), and p is permeability class (1 = very rapid … 6 = very slow). Use the structure and permeability classes derived from the texture class (typically s = 2, p = 3 for these Chernozems).

steps.title: Run RUSLE erosion model
steps.instruction: Input the calculated K‑factor together with the following constant parameters: R‑factor = 320 MJ mm ha⁻¹ h⁻¹ yr⁻¹, C‑factor = 0.40, LS‑factor automatically computed from a digital terrain model (SRTM DEM, cell size 30 × 30 m); use the same soil‑structure (s = 2) and permeability (p = 3) classes for all runs. Perform the modeling in the RUSLE software and record the predicted mean annual soil‑loss values.

steps.title: Statistical analysis of results
steps.instruction: Analyze all obtained data (particle‑size distributions, K‑factors, modeled soil‑loss) with Statistica 12.0 (TIBCO Software Inc., USA).

description: In present study, we suggest to researchers indicate in scientific works (articles, report, etc.) which method was used for RUSLE K-factor calculations, because related with this variations in soil erodibility have an great impact on final soil loss estimations under modeling. Undoubtedly and ideally is provide a validation on standardized runoff plots, and then summarize which method of soil texture determination is more correct for K-factor calculations; however such field works required a long-term observations and labor intensive. Another way is compare and validates result of erosion modeling (with K-factor obtained by different methods) with field erosion data. However, even just field methods (soil-profile truncation, radiocesium technique, etc.) provide errors of 5–40 % in soil erosion rates estimation [40]. Thus, for validation and selection of the “best” RUSLE K-factor estimation method based on soil texture, we will search the data from standardized runoff plots for Chernozems in the Central Russian Upland or will provide such measurements. Possible limitations are mainly related to the methods for determining input parameters of RUSLE K-factor formula (SOC, soil structure and permeability classes) and equipment. For example, for the SOC content determination we used Tyurin approach [22], since other methods, e.g. loss on ignition (LOI) could provide other results, and therefore impact on estimated final K-factor values. Other limitation related to location of Chernozems, for example, we cannot guarantee that our suggestions will be correct on Chernozems with other formation conditions (over-moistened, with very low or very high SOC content, in regions and/or countries different in climate from the Central Russian Upland). During K-factor calculations we used a soil structure code and soil permeability code based on soil texture class [31]; the convertation proposed by Bagarello et al.
